title: CAP, PACELC and consistency models
scopeHtml: Scope: CAP, PACELC, consistency models, quorums, conflict resolution, per-feature choices.

notes.title: Why distributed systems must choose
notes.html:
When data lives on several machines connected by a network, the network can fail, and you must decide what to do during that failure. This is the heart of CAP.

A partition means some nodes cannot talk to others (switch failure, cut cable, overloaded link, long GC pause that looks like a death). In a partition each side must choose: refuse requests (stay consistent) or answer with possibly stale data (stay available).

(The link between Node 1 and Node 2 is the one that breaks.)

Worked example. A bank balance replicated on two nodes. Link breaks. Client A withdraws 80 of 100 on Node 1; client B withdraws 80 on Node 2. If both succeed (available), the balance is -60 after merge. If Node 2 refuses (consistent), B sees an error but money is safe.

Industry examples. Network partitions are not rare: public post-mortems from major clouds and data stores report them regularly. Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen tests have shown many databases losing data or breaking promised guarantees under partitions.

Everyday analogy. Two bank branches whose phone line is cut: they can either stop serving customers or serve them and reconcile later.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing partitions can be ignored on a LAN; they happen.
  • Treating CAP as a menu where you "pick two always".

notes.title: CAP theorem
notes.html:
CAP: in the presence of a network Partition, a system can provide either Consistency or Availability, not both.

  • Consistency (C), linearizability: every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were one copy.
  • Availability (A): every request to a non-failed node gets a (non-error) response, though not necessarily the newest data.
  • Partition tolerance (P): the system continues despite dropped messages between nodes.

Since partitions will happen, real choice is CP vs AP during a partition. When no partition exists, you can have both C and A.

CP examples:  ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase, Spanner (mostly), MongoDB (default majority writes),
              Redis cluster with strict settings (not guaranteed)
AP examples:  Cassandra (tunable), DynamoDB (eventually consistent reads default),
              Riak, CouchDB, DNS

(Classifications are simplifications; many systems are tunable per request.)

Worked example (quorum). 3 replicas, partition isolates 1. The side with 2 nodes holds a majority and keeps serving writes (CP); the isolated single node rejects writes. In an AP design, both sides accept writes and merge later via last-write-wins or vector clocks.

Decision gravity. CP vs AP is a business and data-model decision and effectively a one-way door: application code and invariants (for example "no oversell") assume the choice. Money, inventory counts, leader election: CP. Feeds, likes, carts, presence: AP, accepting repair logic.

Everyday analogy. Two ticket counters selling the last seat with a broken phone line: stop selling (consistent) or keep selling and risk double booking (available).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "CA system" for a distributed database; without P, you are a single node.
  • Using C in CAP as the same C as in ACID (they differ).
  • Saying MongoDB/Cassandra is "just AP/CP" without mentioning tunable settings.

notes.title: Beyond CAP: PACELC
notes.html:
PACELC: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. It captures the day-to-day trade-off CAP ignores: even with no partition, keeping replicas consistent costs latency.

System            If partition   Else (normal)   Label
DynamoDB (eventual) A             L               PA/EL
Cassandra (default) A             L               PA/EL
Cassandra QUORUM    A (partly)    C               tunable
MongoDB (default)   C             C               PC/EC (approx)
Spanner             C             C (pays latency) PC/EC
PNUTS (Yahoo)       C             L               PC/EL

(Labels are from the PACELC paper and later commentary; settings change them; confirm per version.)

Worked example. A write must reach 3 replicas in 3 regions (RTT 80 ms). Waiting for all: 80+ ms latency, strongly consistent. Waiting for 1: ~2 ms, replicas lag by tens of ms. That latency-vs-consistency choice happens on every write, partition or not.

Industry examples. Spanner uses TrueTime and waits out clock uncertainty (a few ms) at commit to get external consistency. DynamoDB offers per-read choice: eventual (cheaper, faster) or strongly consistent (costs 2x read capacity units and higher latency).

Decision gravity. Choosing sync vs async replication is mostly reversible via configuration but changes failure guarantees (RPO) and write latency, so review it per data class.

Everyday analogy. A group chat: waiting for everyone to confirm each message (slow, consistent) or posting right away (fast, some see it later).

Common interview traps.

  • Stopping at CAP when asked about trade-offs in normal operation.
  • Not quantifying latency cost of cross-region sync writes.

notes.title: Consistency models
notes.html:
A consistency model is the contract about what a reader may see. From strongest to weakest:

  • Linearizable (strong): operations appear to happen instantly at one point between call and return; real-time order respected. Reads always see the latest write. Cost: coordination (consensus, quorum, locks).
  • Sequential: all see the same order, not necessarily matching real time.
  • Causal: if A could have influenced B, everyone sees A before B; unrelated writes may appear in different orders.
  • Read-your-writes / session guarantees: you always see your own writes; monotonic reads (never go back in time); monotonic writes; writes-follow-reads.
  • Eventual: if writes stop, replicas converge. No promise on how soon or what you see meanwhile.

Worked example (read-your-writes). User updates profile name on primary; the next page read hits a replica lagging 300 ms and shows the old name. Fixes: read from primary for N seconds after a write, route by a version/LSN token the client carries, or sticky routing for that user. Facebook's early memcache/MySQL setup used "remote marker" tricks for the same issue.

Worked example (monotonic reads). User refreshes twice, hits replica A (up to date) then replica B (behind) and sees data disappear. Fix: pin a session to one replica or carry a minimum version.

Quorum arithmetic. With N replicas, write quorum W, read quorum R: if R + W > N, a read overlaps the latest write (N=3, W=2, R=2). Common configs: W=1,R=N (fast writes), W=N,R=1 (fast reads), W=R=quorum (balanced). Overlap alone does not give linearizability (sloppy quorums, clock-based last-write-wins and concurrent writes can still break it).

# Cassandra per-query consistency (CQL: CONSISTENCY LOCAL_QUORUM) with RF=3 per DC
# LOCAL_QUORUM = 2 of 3 replicas in the local data centre
# Reads + writes at LOCAL_QUORUM: R+W=4 > 3, overlap guaranteed within the DC

Industry examples. Spanner and etcd: linearizable. DynamoDB: eventual by default, strong optional. MongoDB: read concerns local, majority, linearizable and causal sessions. Amazon S3: strongly consistent for reads after writes since December 2020 (it was eventually consistent for overwrites before that).

Decision gravity. Choose per data type: balances and inventory need strong; timelines, counters and caches accept eventual. Weakening later breaks invariants the code assumed; strengthening later costs latency and often a migration.

Everyday analogy. News: a live scoreboard (strong) versus a newspaper tomorrow (eventual); in between, a friend who always repeats what you told them (read-your-writes).

Common interview traps.

  • Using "eventual consistency" to mean "wrong data"; it is a convergence guarantee.
  • Believing R + W > N gives linearizability.
  • Mixing up ACID consistency (constraints hold) with CAP consistency (linearizability).

notes.title: Resolving conflicts in AP systems
notes.html:
If both sides accept writes, you must merge later. Options:

  • Last write wins (LWW): keep the highest timestamp. Simple but loses data and depends on clocks (skew of tens of ms or more).
  • Vector clocks / version vectors: detect true concurrency, then keep siblings for the app to merge (Dynamo's shopping cart merged by union).
  • CRDTs: data types whose merges are commutative and convergent (counters, sets, registers); used in Redis Enterprise, Riak, collaborative editors.
  • Application-level merge or operational transforms for documents.
  • Read repair and anti-entropy (Merkle trees) bring replicas back together; hinted handoff stores writes for a down node.

Worked example. Cart on two nodes: one adds "book", the other adds "pen" during a partition. A set-union merge gives {book, pen}. With LWW, one item vanishes. For a "like" counter, a CRDT G-Counter (one slot per node, merge by max, value = sum) never loses increments.

Industry examples. Amazon Dynamo (vector clocks, cart merge), Cassandra (LWW per cell by default, with timestamps), Riak (siblings, CRDTs), Figma and Google Docs (CRDT or OT).

Decision gravity. Picking LWW is a hidden data-loss decision; choose it only when overwriting is acceptable (sensor reading), not for money.

Everyday analogy. Two people editing the same notes offline and merging later; either pick one version (lose edits) or combine both.

Common interview traps.

  • Using LWW with unsynchronised clocks and calling it safe.
  • Ignoring that clock skew can reorder writes even without a partition.

notes.title: Choosing in a design interview
notes.html:
Decide per feature, not per system. One product uses several consistency levels at once.

Feature                  Need                 Typical choice
Payment / balance        Linearizable         Single-leader SQL, Spanner, CP
Inventory (last unit)    Strong for decrement SQL row lock / conditional write
Order status             Read-your-writes     Primary reads after write
Profile page             Eventual + RYW       Replicas + sticky/version token
News feed, likes         Eventual             Cache, AP store, CRDT counter
Presence, typing         Best effort          In-memory, TTL
Leader election, locks   Linearizable         etcd / ZooKeeper (Raft / Zab)

Answer template: "For X, losing/duplicating means Y. So I need consistency level Z. I pay for it with latency L and lower availability under partition. For W the cost of staleness is small, so I use eventual and accept N ms of lag."

Worked example. E-commerce: product browsing and reviews are eventual from replicas and a cache (staleness up to 60 s is fine). Inventory reservation uses a conditional update UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty > 0 on the primary; payment uses idempotency keys and a single-leader database.

UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'S1' AND qty > 0;  -- 0 rows updated means out of stock

Industry examples. Amazon's retail catalogue is largely eventual while order placement is strict. Uber trip state needs strong consistency per trip (a trip must have exactly one driver) while driver location is best effort.

Decision gravity. The per-feature consistency table is the artefact worth stating in an interview; wrongly assigning "strong everywhere" makes the system slow and costly, "eventual everywhere" makes it incorrect.

Everyday analogy. A shop uses a precise till for money and a rough chalkboard for specials.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring the whole system "CP" or "AP".
  • Not tying the choice to the business cost of a wrong read.
  • Forgetting to mention how you obtain read-your-writes in a replicated setup.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Partitions happen, so the real choice is C or A during a partition (CAP); with no partition, PACELC says latency vs consistency.
  • CAP "C" is linearizability, not ACID consistency; "A" means every live node answers.
  • Models from strong to weak: linearizable, sequential, causal, session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads), eventual.
  • Quorums: R + W > N overlaps the latest write but is not automatically linearizable.
  • AP systems need conflict resolution: LWW (lossy), vector clocks, CRDTs, app merges; use read repair and anti-entropy.
  • Choose consistency per feature by the business cost of a wrong read; money and locks strong, feeds and counters eventual.

questions.promptHtml: What does the CAP theorem actually say, and why is "pick two of three" misleading?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: CAP is quoted by everyone and understood by few. The signal is whether you know what C, A and P mean and when the choice applies.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Partitions will happen on any real network, so P is not optional. CAP says that during a partition each side must either refuse requests to stay consistent, meaning linearizable, or answer with possibly stale data to stay available. With no partition you can have both, so it is a choice made during failure, not a permanent menu."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• C is linearizability: every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were one copy. It is not the C of ACID.
  • A: every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response, not necessarily the newest.
  • P: the system keeps working despite dropped messages between nodes.
Two replicas, link cut.
CP: minority side rejects writes  -> some clients get errors, data stays correct
AP: both sides accept writes      -> everyone is served, replicas diverge, merge later

"CA" is only a single node (no partitions to tolerate). Classifications like "Cassandra is AP, MongoDB is CP" are simplifications: both are tunable per request.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "CA distributed database".
  • Mixing ACID consistency with CAP consistency.
  • Labelling a whole system CP or AP instead of deciding per feature.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Give a CP and an AP example. -> etcd/ZooKeeper (CP), DynamoDB eventual reads or Cassandra at low consistency (AP).
  2. Does CAP say anything about latency? -> No, that is PACELC.
  3. A bank balance replicated on two nodes, link breaks: what do you do? -> Reject the minority side's withdrawals (CP); an AP choice could double-spend.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer recites C, A, P and "choose two". The senior ties it to the failure case, definitions of C and A, and to a per-feature business cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that assumed their cross-AZ link never partitioned saw split-brain writes after a switch failure.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing a shopping app: product browsing and reviews, a cart, inventory reservation for the last unit, payment, "likes" on reviews, and a typing indicator in customer chat. The interviewer says: "Is your system CP or AP?"

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It is AP for scalability" or "CP because data must be correct": a single label for the whole system.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does a wrong read cost for each feature? What staleness is tolerable? Is the system multi-region?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A, design question. I reframe: "I decide per feature."
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Map each feature by cost of a wrong read.
  4. How I'd verify: Write the table, then walk the failure case: what does the user see during a partition?
Feature              Need              Choice
Payment, balance     Linearizable      Single-leader SQL (CP)
Last-unit inventory  Strong decrement  UPDATE ... WHERE qty > 0 on primary
Cart                 Never lose items  AP with merge (union)
Reviews, browsing    Eventual (60 s)   Replicas + cache
Likes                Eventual          CRDT counter
Typing indicator     Best effort       In-memory, TTL
  1. Root cause of the interviewer's question: They want to hear that the choice is tied to business cost.
  2. Fix: Answer template: "For X, a stale or duplicated read means Y, so I need consistency Z and I accept lower availability under partition. For W, staleness is cheap so I use eventual."
  3. Prevention: Document the per-feature consistency table in the design.
  4. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make everything strong (slow and expensive) or everything eventual (incorrect payments).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What does the user see during a partition on payment? -> An error or retry, never a double charge; with idempotency keys the retry is safe.
  • Cart conflict? -> Union merge: a deleted item may reappear; accept that.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an "everything strong" design met a launch-day p99 of 900 ms and was relaxed for feed and counters, keeping strong for payments only.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one label for the system.
  • Hire: per-feature split with reasons.
  • Strong hire: ties to cost of wrong read, partition behaviour and idempotency.

questions.promptHtml: What does PACELC add on top of CAP, and how does it change how you evaluate a database?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most of the time there is no partition. A senior engineer reasons about the everyday latency-versus-consistency cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "If Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency. Even with a healthy network, keeping replicas in sync means waiting for them, which costs latency, so I ask what a write must wait for."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A write that must reach 3 regions with RTTs of 60 and 120 ms waits at least 120 ms if all must ack, 60 ms for a majority, about 2 ms if async. That choice exists on every write.

DynamoDB (eventual)    PA/EL
Cassandra (ONE)        PA/EL
Spanner                PC/EC (pays commit latency)
MongoDB (default)      PC/EC (approx)

Labels depend on settings and version; confirm per system. DynamoDB offers per-read choice between eventual and strongly consistent (strong costs 2x read capacity, higher latency).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Stopping at CAP when asked about everyday trade-offs.
  • Not quantifying cross-region write latency.
  • Treating the labels as fixed instead of per-request settings.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does Spanner get consistency across regions? -> Consensus and TrueTime commit-wait; it pays latency to be consistent.
  2. What do you give up with async replication? -> Recovery point objective: writes in flight are lost if the leader dies.
  3. How do you pick per data class? -> Money strong; feeds eventual; document each.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer repeats CAP. The senior brings the latency numbers, RPO and per-request tuning.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team moved to synchronous cross-region replication for all tables and discovered write p99 tripled; they restricted it to ledger tables.

questions.contextHtml:
A social app serves reads from 3 async MySQL replicas and writes to the primary. Users complain: "I changed my display name, saved successfully, and the profile still shows the old name; after a refresh it is right, sometimes wrong again." Metrics:

replica_lag_ms   p50 40   p99 310   max 2,900 (during batch job)
profile_update   200 OK, redirect to GET /profile
GET /profile     routed round-robin to any replica

Support tickets: 1,100/day.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without sending all reads to the primary.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a cache" or "make replication synchronous". Neither targets the guarantee needed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the problem only for the user's own data (read-your-writes) or also other users seeing stale (acceptable)? Is there a session or user id at the router? How is the replica chosen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: After a write, read that user's data from the primary for 5 s.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) replication lag with replica reads: lag p99 is 310 ms, longer than the redirect time (about 50 ms); (b) a cache holding old values; (c) the intermittent flip-flop is a monotonic reads problem: one request hits a fresh replica, the next a lagging one.
  4. How I'd verify: Log the replica and its replication position for each read; correlate stale reads with Seconds_Behind_Master/GTID position; reproduce right after a save.
  5. Root cause: Round-robin across async replicas gives neither read-your-writes nor monotonic reads.
  6. Fix: Session guarantees: (1) after a write, return the commit position (GTID/LSN) in a cookie; the router sends the next read only to a replica that has reached it, else the primary; (2) or sticky routing of a user to one replica; (3) or primary reads for N seconds after write. Others' views stay eventual.
  7. Prevention: Alert on lag p99 above a threshold; integration test with an artificially lagging replica.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not read everything from the primary (it removes the point of replicas) and not make replication sync for all writes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Replica lag hits 2.9 s during the batch job? -> Route by position token; the primary absorbs those reads; throttle the batch job.
  • Multi-region? -> Keep the token regional and fall back to the home region's primary.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: the team added a 5 s "recently wrote" primary pin keyed by user id; complaints dropped by 95% and primary read load rose only about 3%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds cache or blanket sync replication.
  • Hire: names read-your-writes and fixes with primary pinning or sticky.
  • Strong hire: also monotonic reads, token routing, lag metrics and cost of the primary pin.

questions.contextHtml: A Dynamo-style store has N=5 replicas in one region. Workload: 95% reads, 5% writes, read p99 target 10 ms, write p99 target 30 ms. The team debates (W=5, R=1), (W=3, R=3) and (W=4, R=2). One node is down for patching about 2% of the time and sometimes two are.
questions.promptHtml: Which configuration do you choose and why? What does R + W > N buy you and what does it not?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "R+W>N means strong consistency, so any of them works."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must reads be linearizable or is overlap with the latest write enough? Are writes allowed to fail during patching? Sloppy quorum on?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: All three satisfy R + W > N (6, 6, 6 > 5).
  4. How I'd verify: Availability table:
Config   Writes survive down nodes   Reads survive down nodes   Latency profile
W=5,R=1  0                           4                          slow writes, fastest reads
W=3,R=3  2                           2                          balanced
W=4,R=2  1                           3                          reads wait for 2
  1. Root cause of the decision: With 95% reads, cheap reads are tempting (W=5, R=1), but W=5 makes every write fail when one node is down, which is 2% of the time plus two-down cases.
  2. Fix: Because two nodes are sometimes down, I choose W=3, R=3: it is the only option where neither reads nor writes block with two nodes down. I meet the 10 ms read target with speculative retry (send a third read after a short delay) rather than by weakening W. If two-down never happens, W=4, R=2 is a reasonable read-latency optimisation. Overlap only guarantees a read sees the latest acknowledged write; it does not give linearizability with sloppy quorums, concurrent writes or clock-based LWW.
  3. Prevention: Test with a node killed under load; track the stale-read rate.
  4. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not choose W=5, R=1: any failure blocks all writes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need linearizable reads? -> Add read repair on the read path and a consensus-based or compare-and-set path for those keys.
  • Multi-DC? -> LOCAL_QUORUM in each DC, overlap within the DC.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a W=ALL setting from a benchmark shipped to production; the first rolling patch caused a full write outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: R+W>N means strong.
  • Hire: availability table, rejects W=5.
  • Strong hire: explains what overlap does not give, speculative retry and sloppy-quorum caveat.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the consistency models from linearizable to eventual. Which would you use for a payment ledger, a profile page and a like counter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you can name the intermediate guarantees (causal, session) that make eventual systems usable.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Linearizable: one global real-time order, reads see the latest write. Sequential: one order everybody agrees on, not tied to real time. Causal: cause before effect everywhere. Session guarantees: read-your-writes, monotonic reads. Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop. Ledger: linearizable. Profile: eventual plus read-your-writes. Like counter: eventual, ideally a CRDT."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strong -> weak:   Linearizable > Sequential > Causal > Session guarantees > Eventual
Cost:             coordination (consensus, quorums)   ->    none

Read-your-writes: you see your own writes. Monotonic reads: you never see time go backwards. Monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads order your own operations. Eventual consistency is a convergence promise, not "wrong data". Do not confuse ACID consistency (constraints hold) with CAP's consistency. Real systems: Spanner and etcd offer linearizable reads; DynamoDB defaults to eventual with optional strong; MongoDB has read concerns (local, majority, linearizable) and causal sessions; S3 has been strongly consistent for read-after-write since December 2020.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating eventual with incorrect.
  • Believing R+W>N alone gives linearizability.
  • Mixing ACID C with CAP C.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Sequential vs linearizable? -> Linearizable adds real-time ordering.
  2. How do you implement read-your-writes? -> Version token, primary reads after write, or sticky routing.
  3. Why is causal attractive? -> It avoids global coordination yet prevents "reply before the question" anomalies.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists strong and eventual. The senior fills the middle with session and causal guarantees and attaches each to a feature.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A comment thread showing replies before the parent post on a multi-region store was fixed with causal ordering via version vectors.

questions.contextHtml: An order service must survive the loss of a whole region. Regions: Mumbai (primary users), Singapore (RTT 60 ms from Mumbai), Frankfurt (RTT 120 ms from Mumbai). Orders are about 2,000 writes/s. Product wants "zero lost orders" and checkout p99 under 400 ms, of which 150 ms is already used elsewhere. Options: (A) async replication to the other two, (B) majority sync (Mumbai plus nearest), (C) wait for all three.
questions.promptHtml: Pick one and defend it with numbers. Is it a one-way door?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sync everywhere for safety" without latency or availability numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "zero lost" mean: RPO 0 for a region loss, or just no lost acknowledged orders under single-node failure? Is a 60 ms add acceptable? Can the order be re-created from the payment provider?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Latency added per write: (A) about 2 ms, (B) about 60 ms (Singapore ack), (C) about 120 ms (Frankfurt ack).
  4. How I'd verify: Budget: 400 - 150 = 250 ms available. (B) adds 60 ms, (C) adds 120 ms: both fit. Availability: (C) blocks all writes when any region is unreachable; (B) tolerates one region down; (A) tolerates all but may lose the replication-lag window (for example 100 to 500 ms of orders, about 200 to 1,000 orders at 2,000/s).
  5. Root cause of the trade-off: Each write pays latency for durability; PACELC's else branch.
  6. Fix: Choose (B): quorum across 3 regions (Mumbai + one more), RPO 0 for a single-region loss, 60 ms extra, survives one region down. Reserve (A) for low-value data (carts, analytics).
  7. Prevention: Region-failure drill; alerts on replication ack latency; fall back to async with an explicit alarm if the nearest region is down (and accept RPO >0 knowingly).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not choose (C): it makes availability worse than a single region, since any of three outages blocks checkout.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Singapore is down: what is the write latency now? -> Frankfurt is the second ack: 120 ms; still within budget.
  • One-way door? -> Mostly reversible by config, but it changes the RPO guarantee and everything built on it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team chose wait-for-all and had a 40-minute checkout outage when one region's link degraded, although the other two were healthy.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks sync-all or async without numbers.
  • Hire: chooses majority with latency math.
  • Strong hire: quantifies RPO of async, availability of each option and degradation plan.

questions.contextHtml:
A Cassandra-backed profile service uses client-supplied timestamps (default last-write-wins per cell). Customers report: "I changed my shipping address twice within a minute; the first (wrong) address came back." Logs for one user:

12:00:01.200  app-3  UPDATE addr='B' (ts=1700000001200000)   ack ok
12:00:01.900  app-7  UPDATE addr='C' (ts=1700000001100000)   ack ok
read at 12:00:05 -> addr='B'
chronyc tracking (app-7): System time 0.8 s slow of NTP time

About 0.3% of profile updates are affected.
questions.promptHtml: Explain and fix it. How would you decide whether LWW is acceptable anywhere?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Cassandra is eventually consistent, retry." The data is not delayed; the later write lost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are timestamps client-side or coordinator-side? Are write paths all NTP-synced? Is the field a whole-value overwrite?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the drifting host's NTP; ask affected users to re-save (support script from audit log).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) clock skew: app-7 is 0.8 s slow, so its later write got an earlier timestamp and lost LWW; (b) replica lag: no, the read returns B even after seconds; (c) a bug in app logic.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare writetime(addr) with wall time at ack; chronyc tracking across the fleet; query the audit log ordering.
  5. Root cause: LWW trusts timestamps; skew of 0.8 s inverted two writes 700 ms apart. Skew can reorder writes even with no partition.
  6. Fix: Short term: NTP/chrony with alerting at 50 ms offset. Long term: do not use client timestamps for contended fields; use a single writer per user (route by user id), lightweight transactions / compare-and-set with a version, or a version column that the app increments (IF version = ?).
  7. Prevention: Clock-offset alert; a chaos test skewing a node's clock by 1 s; code review rule "LWW only where overwriting is acceptable".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use LWT (Paxos-based, several round trips) for every write; only for fields where lost updates are unacceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Where is LWW fine? -> Sensor readings, last-seen timestamps, caches.
  • Could you use vector clocks? -> Yes, to detect concurrency and merge or ask the user, at the cost of complexity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a leap-second smear misconfiguration on two hosts caused hundreds of vanished updates before anyone linked them to clocks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames eventual consistency or retries.
  • Hire: identifies clock skew, uses a version/CAS.
  • Strong hire: explains LWW semantics, clock monitoring, scoping LWT and vector-clock alternative.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service runs a primary in Region A and a hot standby in Region B with an automatic failover script: "if the primary does not answer health checks for 20 s, promote B". The WAN link flaps for 90 seconds. Region A stays healthy and keeps serving its clients; B promotes itself and serves its clients. After the link heals:

wallet-A: 41,200 writes during window
wallet-B: 13,800 writes during window
conflicting balances detected: 1,412 wallets
negative balances: 187
questions.promptHtml: What failure mode is this, how do you reconcile now, and how do you redesign?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the failover threshold longer." Longer thresholds only delay split brain.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can clients reach both regions? Is there a third vantage point? Is money involved with idempotency keys?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Demote one side (B), freeze payouts on conflicted wallets, snapshot both logs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Network partition with an unfenced failover (two primaries). Not replication lag; both accepted writes independently.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare the write logs and sequence numbers by wallet; confirm both nodes believed they were primary (leader epoch logs).
  5. Root cause: Failover decided by one side's timeout cannot distinguish a dead primary from a partitioned one. This is CAP: during the partition the design chose availability on both sides for money.
  6. Fix: Reconcile with the transaction logs: replay both and apply conflict rules (idempotency keys, ledger entries are append-only and commutative, balance recomputed); investigate the 187 negative balances manually/with finance policy. Redesign: leader election by quorum across three sites (consensus: Raft/etcd or a managed strongly consistent store); the leader needs a majority, so the minority side stops accepting writes; add fencing tokens (epoch numbers) so a stale primary's writes are rejected by storage.
  7. Prevention: Network partition game days; invariants test (no negative balance); alert on two nodes claiming leadership.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not choose automatic failover with two nodes only. The CP choice means the minority region rejects writes during a partition; for a wallet that is correct.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Region A is the minority (only 1 of 3 sites)? -> It stops writes; clients fail over to the majority side.
  • Why a witness in a third site? -> To break ties; two sites cannot form a majority after a split.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a payments team's two-node "auto promote" caused double payouts during a flaky link; they moved the ledger to a consensus store and kept caches AP.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: longer timeout.
  • Hire: names split brain, quorum leader election and fencing.
  • Strong hire: reconciliation plan, invariants, witness site and CP for money.

questions.promptHtml: If an AP database accepts writes on both sides of a partition, how are the conflicts resolved afterwards? Compare last-write-wins, vector clocks and CRDTs, and say when each is appropriate.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: AP is easy to say; the cost is the merge logic. Seniors know each strategy's failure mode.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LWW keeps the highest timestamp: simple but loses data and trusts clocks. Vector clocks detect that two writes were truly concurrent and keep siblings for the application to merge. CRDTs are data types whose merge is commutative, associative and idempotent, so replicas converge without coordination: counters, sets. Read repair, hinted handoff and Merkle-tree anti-entropy bring replicas together."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cart: node1 adds book, node2 adds pen during the partition
LWW         -> one item lost
Vector clk  -> siblings {book},{pen} -> app merges (union)
OR-Set CRDT -> {book, pen}
Like counter: G-Counter, slot per node, merge = max per slot, value = sum

Vector clocks grow with writers and need pruning. CRDTs constrain the data model: a "balance that cannot go negative" is not a plain CRDT. Dynamo's cart used union merge, which can resurrect a deleted item. Collaborative editors use CRDTs or operational transforms.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• LWW with unsynchronised clocks called safe.
  • Using a CRDT where an invariant (no oversell) must hold.
  • Forgetting anti-entropy: merge also needs a detection mechanism.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is LWW acceptable? -> When overwriting is harmless: sensor readings, last-seen.
  2. How does hinted handoff work? -> A coordinator keeps writes for a down node and replays them when it returns.
  3. Why is a negative-balance constraint hard in AP? -> It needs coordination; use escrow or reserve budgets per node.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "use LWW". The senior chooses per data type and knows the loss model.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team using LWW for a shared notes field lost edits; switching to sibling storage and a merge UI resolved it.

questions.contextHtml:
A Dynamo-style store (N=3, W=2, R=2) is used for a feature-flag service. During a rack outage, an engineer toggled a flag off. The write was acknowledged. For 6 minutes afterwards some read requests (R=2) still returned the old "on" value, and users continued to see the feature. Notes from the incident:

write coordinator: "W=2 satisfied: replicas n4 (hinted), n2"
preference list for key: n1, n2, n3  (n1 and n3 were in the failed rack)
reads: coordinator contacted n1 and n3 after rack restored -> both stale
hinted data on n4 delivered 6 min later
questions.promptHtml: R + W = 4 > N = 3, so why was the read stale? What do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A bug in the database." The behaviour is by design with sloppy quorums.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is sloppy quorum enabled? What is the hint delivery policy? Does the flag service need linearizability?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Force the flag value (write at ALL / repair), purge caches, run read repair.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) sloppy quorum: the write was acked by n2 and a stand-in n4 outside the preference list, so the quorum overlap guarantee against {n1, n2, n3} is gone; (b) clock-based LWW misordering; (c) cache TTL.
  4. How I'd verify: Inspect where each replica stored the write; query each replica's value; check whether the coordinator used a hinted node.
  5. Root cause: R + W > N only guarantees overlap if reads and writes use the same N nodes. Sloppy quorum trades that for write availability; a read of {n1, n3} did not intersect the write set {n2, n4}.
  6. Fix: For control-plane data like flags, use a strong store (etcd/Consul-type consensus) or strict quorum (no hinting) at the cost of write unavailability during a rack outage; and fast hint delivery with read repair as a mitigation. Add a version number and have clients reject lower versions.
  7. Prevention: Per-data-class consistency table; tests that kill racks during writes and verify reads.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not blanket-disable sloppy quorum for a shopping-cart-style data set, where write availability matters more than overlap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would R=3 help? -> Reading all three would hit n2 and see the new value, but breaks under any failure.
  • Is overlap enough for linearizability? -> No: concurrent writes, LWW and read repair races can still violate it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a flag rollback "did not take" for 6 minutes during a rack loss; the flag service moved to a consensus-backed store and kept the AP store for user preferences.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: calls it a database bug.
  • Hire: explains sloppy quorum breaks the overlap guarantee.
  • Strong hire: moves control-plane data to a consensus store, discusses hint delivery and per-data-class choice.

questions.contextHtml: The interviewer says: "Make inventory highly available across two regions, and never oversell." Flash sales sell 500 units of a SKU in 2 minutes with 40k requests/s peak. Regions: US and EU, inter-region RTT 90 ms. Customers are 60% US, 40% EU.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a multi-master database with eventual consistency and fix oversells later," or silently choosing CP and ignoring availability.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does "available" mean a region keeps selling during an inter-region partition? Is overselling by 1 to 2 units acceptable with a compensating action (backorder, voucher)? Is stock per SKU small (500) or huge (millions)? Is the cost of an oversell high (limited collectible) or low (commodity)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A. I state the conflict: the last-unit decrement is a linearizable operation; under a partition I cannot have both strict no-oversell and both regions selling (CAP).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: (a) single home region per SKU (CP): all decrements go to one primary, EU pays 90 ms, if the home is cut off EU cannot sell that SKU; (b) split stock: allocate 300 US, 200 EU, each region decrements locally with no coordination; rebalance by transfer; partitions leave each region selling its share, no oversell; (c) multi-master with compensation (AP): fast, can oversell.
  4. How I'd verify: Model unsold stock stranding: if EU sells out its 200 while US has 100 left, a transfer takes about 90 ms plus coordination; simulate demand split.
  5. Root cause of the tension: Invariant "qty >= 0" needs coordination.
  6. Fix: I propose (b) escrow/budget allocation with conditional decrements UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku=? AND qty > 0 in each region, periodic rebalancing, and region-level availability under partition. For rare high-value SKUs use (a); for cheap items use (c) with compensation.
  7. Prevention: Reconciliation job; invariant alerts; load test the flash sale; oversell rate dashboard.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not claim "both" without stating the partition behaviour; and not allocate stock 50/50 blindly, since it strands inventory.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• During a partition, a region exhausts its share? -> It stops selling that SKU (sold out locally) until the link heals, which is the cost of no oversell.
  • Where do reservations expire? -> TTL on holds in the owning region.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a limited drop used one global counter, making the EU p99 checkout 400 ms slower; a per-region stock budget with rebalancing fixed it and kept zero oversells.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: promises both without trade-off.
  • Hire: asks clarifying questions and names CAP conflict.
  • Strong hire: proposes home-region vs stock budgets vs compensation by SKU class with numbers and partition behaviour.
